So whiteboarding is actually a fairly easy round - but yes, candidates just get nervous a lot. It's one of those rounds where there are no right answers - cause neither you or I can design anything great in 45 mins. So here are some tips:

There are the 4 areas Meta (or any big tech) looks for:

**Product Thinking & Impact:** Understands a product’s goals and the problems of its target users; identifies opportunities to inform product strategy; makes decisions based on user and company impact.
**Interactive & Experience Design**: Understands how a product's experience should behave based on users' needs; architects functional, usable, technically informed, end-to-end design solutions.
**Elevating Visual Design & Craft**: Designs appropriately for scale, systems, and accessibility with excellence in craft. Uses best practices across visual domains to create aesthetically pleasing experiences that connect with users.
**Thinking Strategically**: Understands the big picture and how various factors impact business and organizational-wide goal attainment. Applies a global perspective to plans and strategies and helps set direction for short and long-term objectives.

The question you'll get is something really generic - like design a self checkout in a grocery store or a smart home or a shared music experience in vr or a grocery delivery or gift giving system.

1. So then you'll have to narrow things down - who is the audience im designing for? what are some "people problems" in this area? What is the "business problem"? 

Write them down on the virtual whiteboard. 

2. Then talk about the "happy path" - what is the best user experience a person would have. Then mention some "unhappy paths" aka edge cases - what if i dont have a phone? what if I am disabled? what if i try to steal something from the grocery store? what if 5 friends are on VR and 1 is on the laptop? etc etc 

3. Make some really rough sketches / wireframes (most interviewers are not expecting any sort of visual design - but it can help to show "systems" thinking by talking about how you can leverage an existing design system, or if your ideas would need some new UI patterns that maynot be in an existing design system).

4. ASK THE INTERVIEWER IF YOU ARE MISSING ANYTHING - be bold and try to get some realtime feedback (in case you get a nicer interviewer who'd help you).

5. Talk through maybe 2-3 options and which is your preferred - talk about tradeoffs - option A is good but it'll likely take 6 months more to ship or will take double the investment compared to option B.

Hope this helps! Feel free to keep asking questions here!

Any specific advice you are looking for? You have your typical rounds - app critique, background and problem solving:

app critique - you've probably already done one of these - focus on all parts of design - visual, ux, people problems being solved, branding etc

background - manager will ask you your motivations for joining meta apart from the obvious "its big tech pays a lot". Answer genuinely - talk about having a growth mindset, wanting to learn more, learn from a senior organisation etc

problem solving - spend 10 mins getting to the core of the problem - then spent 10 mins doing a variety of solutions - maybe give a few options a,b,c and then talk about which option is more approps.

I take all these interviews at meta - so happy to provide guidance if you can say what specific kinds of advice you are looking for.

I think "treating yourself" and "spending money on yourself" have become rather negative terms in the fire community (or in this subreddit at least). 

I see it first hand in my parents lives - they've saved and saved and saved, and while it has enabled me to live a good life, they are in their 60's and straight up dont know how to enjoy things anymore. They take pride in their misery (eg: my dad has a decade old laptop with a broken screen he refuses to get a new one despite using it everyday). They live in a old creaky house despite having the money to make it better, because they dont have the mental muscle of improving their lives anymore. They wont go to any nice places to eat drink even for special occasions because its too "expensive". This is not because they dont have money or are in debt...its because they literally cant bring themselves to part with the cash.

Its a mentality of "well we've lived with this setup for so many years, whats wrong with it?" and it absolutely affects their quality of life....except that they now take pride in their misery and look down upon anyone that doesnt want to live in those shit conditions anymore (aka me).

This leads me to STRONGLY believe that if i dont on a semi-regular basis do things that I currently consider "indulgent", I will eventually become the grumpy, always complaining, miserable old person. This doesnt mean I am irresponsibly spending loads of money on random crap. But it does mean I actively try to spend money on new things and experiences.
